changes.before: A high-rise factory employs a large, economically dependent workforce among substantial combustible production material. Management has legitimate concerns about theft, unauthorised departure and production control. At least some exit access is tightly controlled during work, and the factory lacks modern automatic fire suppression. Management must decide whether property/production controls may compromise emergency egress or whether worker escape and fire protection take priority.
changes.after: A high-rise factory employs a large, economically dependent workforce among substantial combustible production material. Management has legitimate concerns about theft, unauthorised departure and production control. Exit doors have locks, but the supplied inspection account found them unlocked during its visit. Routine door status, individual knowledge and the completeness of fire protection remain uncertain. Management must decide whether property/production controls may compromise emergency egress or whether worker escape and fire protection take priority.
changes.rationale: Use reported inspection observations, not later escape or trial events, for door status. Do not infer routine locking, personal knowledge, absence of sprinklers or proven security-equivalent alternatives from incomplete accounts. Keep the selected policy unchanged and mark its unsupported historical premise as an admission blocker.

changes.before: The Triangle Shirtwaist Company operates a large garment factory on the upper floors of a New York building. The workforce is predominantly young immigrant women working among large quantities of cloth, paper patterns and other combustible material. Management has legitimate concerns about theft, unauthorised departures and production control. Testimony and later records indicate that at least some exit-door access was controlled/locked during work and that the factory lacked modern sprinkler protection. The question is how management should balance property/production controls against emergency escape and fire risk before any catastrophic fire is assumed.

before: The case should not be reduced to the slogan that the owners deliberately intended worker deaths. The Moral Code question is whether the system foreseeably subordinated worker safety to control/cost interests when less dangerous alternatives existed.
The criminal acquittal illustrates the difference between proving an individual's guilt beyond reasonable doubt and evaluating whether a workplace policy/system meets a preventive moral standard.

This case is retained as an MC-07 non-extraction test: private benefits such as theft prevention, labour discipline or avoided safety expenditure do not justify exporting catastrophic risk to low-power workers when safer means are reasonably available.
